case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

     performance.

     message.

   Scoring:

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.answer: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions
case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.

  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.
